definition: The value function of an optimization problem gives the value attained by the objective function at a solution, while only depending on the parameters of the problem.
details: In a controlled dynamical system, the value function represents the optimal payoff of the system over the interval [ t , t 1 ] {\displaystyle [t,t_{1}]} when started at the time- t {\displaystyle t} state variable x ( t ) = x {\displaystyle x(t)=x} . If the objective function represents some cost that is to be minimized, the value function can be interpreted as the cost to finish the optimal program, and is thus referred to as "cost-to-go function." In an economic context, where the objective function usually represents utility, the value function is conceptually equivalent to the indirect utility function. In a problem of optimal control, the value function is defined as the supremum of the objective function taken over the set of admissible controls. explainer.lead: The value function collapses an entire optimization problem into the best objective value achievable from a given situation. It matters because it lets a planner judge states and choices without re-solving the whole problem each time.

tiers.eli5: Think of a trip-planning app that tells you the best possible total cost from wherever you are standing right now — that number, as a function of your current spot, is the value function.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it in dynamic programming and reinforcement learning as the quantity to estimate, often as a cost-to-go when the objective is a cost to minimize. A common pitfall is assuming it stays valid after the problem's parameters change, when it must be recomputed.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, V(p) = the objective function value attained at an optimal solution, depending only on the problem parameters p. In a controlled dynamical system it is the optimal payoff over [t, t1] starting from state x(t) = x; it is called the cost-to-go when the objective is a cost to be minimized. Limits: it is defined with respect to a fixed problem parameterization and a specified horizon.

explainer.example: In a controlled dynamical system started at time t in state x, the value function gives the optimal payoff over the interval [t, t1]; if the objective is a cost, it is the cost to finish the optimal program.
